doc.title: Ben Sidran interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 15, 2023

chapter: Jazz life and the state of jazz
title: Is jazz in trouble? Academia versus the road
summary: Style comes from recovering from mistakes; learning from a syllabus and not on the bus has changed the tradition.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: You spoke about how their emotions were amplified closer to the surface, it reminded me I had a note to myself that forty years ago, during “Jazz Class,” your presentation, you said, “Jazz is in trouble partly because of the long form and our increasingly short attention span.” But also that it “brings out emotions that people tend to want to avoid.”
You did. I have some quotes here. But if jazz was in trouble forty years ago, where is it now?

Well you know there’s a lot of discussion about that today. And it centers on the fact that we have so many people learning it in academic situations and what’s the impact of that? I mean and that goes right to the question of style, where does style come from? You know almost everybody, when they get down to it, will say that style comes from how you recover from what you perceive to be as mistakes. They’re not mistakes, they’re opportunities. And it’s in the recovery of playing something you didn’t intend or whatever that your sound comes out and your style comes out. But if you learn the music as part of a syllabus, if you are in fact graded on the music, that’s going to give you an entirely different relationship to the experience of playing music. So while today we have brilliant young players, I mean every instrument — piano players, saxophone players, they’ve never been better prepared to play this music and with the Internet everything’s available. It’s incredible. Yet something has been disrupted in the tradition. And it has

something to do with being a sideman and learning out on the road and being on a bus with other musicians. It has something to do with the grit that was in the music that tends not to be in the music that way anymore because well it’s often said, if you spend eight hours a day in a practice room, you’re going to sound like you’re in a practice room. If you spend eight hours a day hanging out with musicians and riding on the bus like they used to do, that’s going to affect how you sound as well. So I wouldn’t say jazz is in trouble, because there are more people playing it today than ever before. I would say that just as in all evolutionary processes eventually you start to get a different kind of animal. The jazz that’s played by young people today for example tends to be highly calculated, like they like to play — kids today like to play with meter and rhythm instead of, you know 4/4 was disrupted after fifty years by 3/4 that took fifty years to play a waltz. Jazz musicians were not that interested in 15, 17 time signatures. But you know after the sixties and Coltrane and everybody there was only so much you could do to do something new. He had extended the harmony and extended the rhythm as far as you can, so you start playing with the forms. And the more you play with the forms, you know, well and people would say well I’m being myself, I’m extending my reach. But at the same time, it’s not swinging. And that’s a big issue today.
